# Records from the Italian Military Tribunal in Mogadishu (1915–1941): Archival Note

# Iman Mohamed

Department of History, University of Minnesota, Minneapolis, MN, USA Email: moha0489@umn.edu

# Abstract

In Somalia Italiana, Africans and Arabs employed in the security forces were critical to the expansion and maintenance of the colonial state. Despite their significance, there is little research on these soldiers due to the scarcity of archival records and oral histories that sheds light on their lives and labor in the colonial military. This article examines colonial military tribunal records, the only available archive with substantive information on individual soldiers, and suggests possible themes for future research.

## Résumé

En Somalia italiana, des Africains et des Arabes employés dans les forces de sécurité se sont montrés critiques de l’expansion et de la continuation de l’Etat colonial. Cet article examine les archives du tribunal militaire, les seules archives contenant des informations significatives sur des soldats individuels, et suggère de possibles futurs thèmes de recherches.

Keywords: Italian colonialism; military law; colonial soldiers; Somalia

Africans and Arabs in the security forces included the askari (regular soldiers), gogle and dubat (irregular soldiers), and zaptié (military police).2 Along with the civil administration, the Italian colonial security forces were among the largest employers of native workers and an important institution in the commodification of labor during the colonial period.3 However, unlike the case of the Eritrean soldiers in the Italian colonial troops, research on soldiers in and from Somalia Italiana has been rather underdeveloped.4 Thisstark gap in the literature isin part a result of the paucity of archival records about these soldiers. In the Italian military archives, native5 soldiers appear only as numbers or data points in the few military reports that survived, without comprehensive information on individual service records. Outside of formal archives, there was no systematic attempt to collect oral historiesofsurvivingveteranswhenmanyofthemcontinued toreceivepensionsat the Italian embassy in Mogadishu before the start of the Somali Civil War.6

Absent firsthand accounts of the lives and trajectories of these soldiers, the most important archival depository for researchers studying native soldiers in Somalia is the collection of judgments from the military tribunal of Mogadishu. These documents form part of military tribunal records from Italian East Africa (Africa orientale italiana) housed in the Italian Central State Archive (Archivio centrale dello Stato). The original records were transferred to this archive by the Military Attorney General’s Office (Procura generale militare) between the 1970s and the late 1990s.7 There is a total of thirty-three files in the archival collection. For those interested in the military or legal history of Italian colonialism, this archive is an invaluable source that has yet to be fully utilized.9 It is the most comprehensive archival record of courts in Somalia Italiana during the colonial era.10 It is also an important source for labor and social history, enabling historians to understand the lives of soldiers and police beyond troop numbers, battalion names and locations, and tactical maneuvers, as is available in existing military reports.11 These legal records have their limitations: the voices of individual soldiers are mediated through interpreters, clerks, advocates, procedural rules, and the biases of military judges.12 Nonetheless, these tribunal cases contain a wealth of information that can shed light on how individuals were recruited, their lives before and during their military service, and their role in colonial administration. This archival note is divided in two parts. The first part offers an analysis of the records from the military tribunal in Mogadishu and explains the basic structure of the court’s judgments. The second part probes the historiographical possibilities that these records can offer for the study of the social, environmental, legal, and broader colonial history of Somalia Italiana.

## The Cases

The application of the Italian military penal code was extended to the colony of Somalia Italiana from the earliest period of Italian occupation.13 The military tribunals that applied this code were initially established on an ad-hoc basis.14 The first permanent military tribunal in Mogadishu was instituted with the promulgation of the civil legal code for the colony.15 Both Italian and native soldiers, as well as Italian noncommissioned officers, were subject to the jurisdiction of this court as well as to military penal and disciplinary codes.16 Civilians were also tried in the military tribunal in relation to crimes that had tenuous connections to the military.17 For example, when the colony was at war, the military could seize property from civilians for the war effort. A number of pastoralists were brought before the war tribunal when they refused to give up their livestock.18 In addition, because the colony’s security forces (zaptié) were tasked with enforcing forced labor conscription, those who refused to be recruited to work on Italian-owned plantations or as corvée labor for the construction of infrastructure could be tried in military courts.19 These are only some of the many different ways that civilians ended up in the military tribunals.20

The permanent military tribunal in Somalia Italiana was located in the capital, including after the colony was incorporated into Italian East Africa following the Ethiopian campaign.21 Aside from exceptional circumstances, all transgressions of military law in Somalia were therefore tried in Mogadishu. This meant that detained individuals could be incarcerated for long periods while awaiting transport to the capital.22

The colony’s governor appointed the judges that oversaw these cases.23 The tribunal was composed of a president, a rapporteur judge (giudice relatore), and several military officers, as well as a court clerk and a public prosecutor. The judicial panel of each case was formed by a president and three judges. The judges were senior military officers in the colonial forces of lieutenant rank or higher.24 The investigating judge (giudice istruttore) on each panel who conducted the investigation on behalf of the court was the local vice prosecutor of the colonial military. There were also interpreters for cases involving African and Arab soldiers.25

When considering the volume of cases that the tribunal adjudicated per day, it may be concluded that trial hearings were relatively quick. Giorgio Rochat found a similar trend in his investigation of two thousand cases in Italian military tribunals during the Second World War, with those courts handling approximately six cases per day.26 In Somalia Italiana, at the height of the Italian invasion of Ethiopia (1935–36), the military tribunal’s case volume increased significantly and there were occasionally more than a dozen cases tried on a single day. This was accompanied by gubernatorial and military decrees legalizing speedy trials, confiscation of property, and suspended sentences due to the colony’s state of war.27 Based on available records, the tribunal adjudicated approximately two to four cases per day.28

The accessible documents in the military tribunal collection are the judgmentsof the court. Each one contains: (1) information on the accused (name, parents’ names, where they were born, age, clan or ethnic background, religion, military rank and regiment, whether detained or free); (2) the charges brought by the military prosecutor; (3) a summary of the incident(s) at the heart of the case and information onthe investigationbythe police or court; (4)summaryof whatoccurred during the public hearing (e.g., testimony of the accused and any witnesses, the arguments of

In some cases where the accused was a fugitive, the court used a form to grant a default judgment against the accused. This was especially the case for desertion charges when the accused was still on the run. The sentences given by the tribunal ranged from fines and a few months in prison to the death penalty. During the Ethiopian campaign, many punishments were suspended, and some were granted amnesty after the end of the war. Italians could make an appeal to the supreme military tribunal in Rome.29 In rare cases when the court imposed the death penalty, the governor could intervene and suspend the sentence.30

## Historiographical possibilities

Although they are not verbatim transcripts of court proceedings or investigations, the judgments alone have a wealth of information hitherto unknown about military life, native soldiers, and Italian colonialism in Somalia more broadly. For example, the biographical information contained in the judgments gives a sense of the diversity (or lack thereof) of military recruitment to the colonial security forces. Using racial criteria, the colonial state restricted enlistment to so-called “martial” or “warrior” clans. However, the judgments demonstrate far greater diversity in the actual composition of the security forces.31 In official colonial discourse, still based on this racial criteria, there was a strong push to recruit people from “servile” backgrounds into the engineering corps (corpo del genio) or porterage due to their alleged “greater physical strength and habit of heavy labor.”32 However, the cases involving soldiers from this corps show that people from all Somali clan groups worked within it, regardless of their place in the indigenous racialized social hierarchy. Similarly, other “martial” regiments also had people from so-called “servile” or nonmartial clans, thus belying the notion that Italians limited military recruitment to a certain segment of the Somali population. The cases can thus illuminate how colonial racial ideas were applied in practice, both in regard to the racialized social hierarchy of the colonized as well as between Italians and colonized subjects.33

The tribunal records also offer significant insight into the legal regime in the colony. In his treatise on colonial law in Somalia Italiana, chief judge Guglielmo Ciamarra emphasized that colonial courts had the goal of reconciling the different legal orders existing in the colony in order to “safeguard the moral authority of the law” and, by extension, that of the colonial state.34 Military law was not exempt from this obligation to mediate different moral and political rationales in order to uphold colonial public order. Indeed, it was the military police – the zaptié and Carabinieri – that was charged with policing duties in the colony. The military tribunal also had overlapping jurisdiction with civilian courts, which could result in different outcomes for accused soldiers.35 Although both legal codes incorporated the principle of protecting the legitimacy of the colonial state, it was only civilian courts that included native intermediaries, namely qadis (Muslim jurists) and state-employed native chiefs (capi stipendiati), in the adjudication while military tribunals had no colonized subjects in their judicial panels.36 The jurisdictional distinction was extremely sensitive in relation to criminal offenses that had severe penalties under Italian law but minor or no penalties under customary or Islamic law. The military tribunal usually attenuated the penalties in the military penal code when applied to native soldiers by referencing article 36 of the colonial legal code: “when the guilty is a colonial subject, the judicial authority, in the application of pecuniary criminal laws and in any other kind of law or regulation, can apply lower sentences than the normal minimums.”37 The court further justified this with allusions to a civilizational or racial defect that divided colonized and Italian soldiers, with the latter being the intended target of the Italian military penal code. It is not only that the tribunal judgments involved racist ideas39 in the legal reasoning, but it is also a recognition of the limited power of the court or state to impose colonial hegemony on a population that had different understandings of legal norms and legitimacy. The judgments also offer a unique perspective on military life inside and outside of barracks and encampments. Why did soldiers enlist? How did they survive the brutal conditions of war and expanding colonial occupation? Despite the significant historiographic interest in the Italian invasion and occupation of Ethiopia, scholars have not sufficiently examined the southern front of the war, Somalia Italiana, and the experience of soldiers, porters, and other workers who were part of that war effort. The bulk of the tribunal cases in the archive begin with the mobilization for the war and could offer scholars material to understand how the state organized the colonial economy and colonized population for the war effort, above all in the process of mobilizing and recruiting new soldiers and workers. In the early years of the war, desertion was one of the most common charges that the military prosecutor brought against native soldiers.40 This was a reflection of the state’s need to embark on a mass mobilization of soldiers and other workers for the war, which might have lowered their standards for military recruits. Although there was no mandatory conscription, once soldiers enlisted, they could not leave the barracks or their divisions without prior authorization.41 These desertion charges applied both to those who did not respond to the December 1934 mobilization order for discharged troops and to those who deserted after being recruited for this war. The cases thus reveal some features of the colonial situation in that period. For example, the time it took for soldiers to be found after they were declared deserters by their unit gives us a sense of the scale and degree of colonial occupation in different parts of the territory. Life in the military, as the deserters attested, was often difficult. This was because the colonial military, like the rest of the colonial state, operated on a limited budget subsidized by the metropole.46 Therefore, the “troops had to always be able to live, maneuver and operate for [long periods] of time … lacking provisions for their [daily] needs.”47 Despite Italian military officers believing that Somali pastoralists were ideal soldiers because they had a naturally austere endurance due to their traditional arid environmental conditions, there are many cases where soldiers refused orders or deserted because they were hungry.48 In one case, the court dismissed a dubat soldier’s claim that he deserted because he had never been fed at the military camp and found the “justifications [to be] manifestly childish and cannot be taken into any consideration given the traditional sobriety of the native.”49 The drastic food insecurity experienced by colonial subjects also had an impact on the military both in terms of recruitment and in the life of soldiers once they enlisted. broke out after soldiers working as drivers refused orders to unload the trucks at their destination because they were too hungry to do work after a long drive.50 This theme of food insecurity is a critical one in regional eco-social history due to the arid and drought-prone ecosystems of the Somali territories.51 Military planners were keenly aware that it was precisely these conditions – including major droughts and famines in the 1920s and 1930s – that compelled many men to seek waged labor in the first place. Reading these cases can give historians a richer understanding of the quotidian impacts of changing environmental and economic conditions of the last century. Timothy Parson’s argument that “the colonial African soldiery was a kind of labor aristocracy” that accrued material benefit in exchange for military discipline has a lot of resonances in the history of Somalia Italiana.52 It is in these cases that we learn, however, that despite desiring the social and material benefits of military labor, soldiers also resented the racial, social, and political implications of military discipline and obedience.53 The training recruits received was supposed to inculcate them with a new subjectivity as workers and soldiers.54 The regulation for native troops specified extra-judicial punishments that could be applied by superior Italian and native officers.55 One of the most common ones – referenced time and again in cases involving disobedience or insubordination – was i ceppi, referring to the practice of putting the ankles of an individual in wooden blocks that were then chained with a padlock, thus restricting their movement. The regulations specified that this punishment could be applied for one to five days for a duration of twelve hours in fourhour intervals. In a number of cases, soldiers were brought before the court on charges of insubordination, refusal of orders, defamation, or desertion for contesting this punishment.56 In addition, soldiers revolted against many other forms of discipline – from the imposition of flogging at the start of the Italian

In addition to contributing to our understanding of colonial history, these legal records can be useful to scholarship on colonial legacies in anti-colonial liberation struggles and postcolonial martial law. As the historiography of anticolonial liberation struggles in other African contexts have shown, veterans of colonial military forces drew upon their military sacrifice to make moral claims upon their former colonial masters.59 The role of veterans from the Italian colonial military is conspicuously absent in the recent literature on decolonization in Somalia despite there being a strong veterans organization that advocated for Italy’s return to Somalia in the post-World War II peace settlement and eventually won pensions for veterans and their families.60 These legal records, particularly mutiny cases, could serve as a helpful companion to the British and Italian archival records from the 1940s and 1950s to understand the impact military service may have had on soldiers’ modes of solidarity and resistance.61 The legacy of Italian military doctrine and discipline also extends to shape the military junta that ruled Somalia for most of the second half of the twentieth century.62 For postcolonial military and political historiography, these colonialera legal records could shed light on the military culture and environment in which leaders like President Mohamed Siad Barre, a former zaptié, were formed.

subsection of soldiers: the defining feature of military life is discipline, and most soldiers remain within the bounds of military law.63 In addition, most transgressions of military discipline never give rise to a legal case. As exceptional as these cases may be, however, these tribunal records are invaluable for studying everything from social relations within the military to the broader structural dynamics of colonial rule. This is even more so in the case of Somalia Italiana where the archival record on military aspects of colonial rule is sparse, and oral history has not been systematically collected. These military tribunal records are therefore an important resource for deciphering the history of African and Arab soldiers in Somalia Italiana.
